title: Quickstart
description: Get your first governed AI response in under 5 minutes.
content:
Quickstart

Raptor is a deterministic governance substrate for AI applications. Every AI response passes through classification, policy enforcement, and cryptographic attestation before it reaches the user.

This guide covers two paths: cloud signup and self-hosted Docker.

Cloud


Sign up at raptor.dev with Google, GitHub, Microsoft, or email.
Create an organization and connect at least one AI provider (Anthropic recommended).
Copy your API key from Settings. It starts with rpt_.


Your base URL is https://api.raptor.dev.

Self-Hosted (Docker)

Prerequisites


Docker and Docker Compose v2+
At least one AI provider API key (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, or Together AI)


Setup

git clone https://github.com/pjamesiii/raptor.git && cd raptor
cp .env.example .env

Edit .env and set two required values:

RAPTOR_ACCESS_TOKEN=a-strong-random-token
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

Start the stack:

docker compose up -d

Three services come up:

| Service | Port | Purpose ||---------|------|---------|| Control Panel | localhost:4000 | API and workspace UI || MCP Server | localhost:4001 | Claude Desktop / Cursor integration || PostgreSQL | localhost:5432 | Governance event store |

Verify the stack is healthy:

curl http://localhost:4000/api/health
{"status":"ok"}

Send your first governed message

curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/api/chat \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Raptor-Token: your-access-token" \
  -d '{"message": "Is this deployment verified?"}'

For cloud, replace localhost:4000 with api.raptor.dev and use your rpt_ API key:

curl -X POST https://api.raptor.dev/api/chat \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer rpt_your_api_key" \
  -d '{"message": "Is this deployment verified?"}'

The response includes:


reply -- the AI's governed response text
trust_boundary -- classification: confirmed, executed, retrieved, likely, or uncertain
segments -- per-claim trust boundaries within the response
decision_support -- confidence le

description: Install Raptor via Docker Compose, build from source, or sign up for cloud.
content:
Installation

Three ways to run Raptor: Docker Compose (recommended for most teams), build from source, or cloud.

Option 1: Docker Compose (recommended)

Prerequisites


Docker Engine 24+ and Docker Compose v2+
At least one AI provider API key (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, or Together AI)


Steps

Clone the repository and create your environment file:

git clone https://github.com/pjamesiii/raptor.git && cd raptor
cp .env.example .env

Edit .env and set the required variables:

# Required
RAPTOR_ACCESS_TOKEN=a-strong-random-token
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

Optional: additional providers
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
GEMINI_API_KEY=...
TOGETHER_API_KEY=...

Optional: Clerk SSO (omit for token-only auth)
CLERK_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...
CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_live_...
CLERK_DOMAIN=your-app.clerk.accounts.dev

Start the stack:

docker compose up -d

This starts three services:

| Service | Port | Description ||---------|------|-------------|| control-panel | 4000 | API server and workspace UI || mcp-server | 4001 | MCP protocol server for Claude Desktop / Cursor || postgres | 5432 | PostgreSQL 16 with governance event store |

Database migrations run automatically on startup via the migrate service.

Verification

Run all three health checks to confirm the stack is operational:

# Liveness — confirms the process is running
curl http://localhost:4000/api/health
{"status":"ok"}

Readiness — confirms the database connection is live
curl http://localhost:4000/api/ready
{"status":"ready"}

Dependencies — per-dependency status
curl http://localhost:4000/api/health/dependencies
{"postgres":"ok","anthropic":"ok"}

All three should return HTTP 200. If /api/ready fails, check that PostgreSQL is healthy:

docker compose ps
docker compose logs postgres

git pull && docker compose build && docker compose up -d

Migrations run automatically on restart.

title: Authentication
description: Authenticate with Raptor using Clerk SSO, API keys, or the Founder Key.
content:
Authentication

Raptor supports three authentication modes. Use whichever fits your context.

| Mode | Use case | Header ||------|----------|--------|| Clerk SSO | Production workspace users | Browser session cookie (automatic) || API keys | Programmatic access, CI/CD, integrations | Authorization: Bearer rpt_... || Founder Key | Development, emergency access, bootstrap | X-Raptor-Founder-Key: ... |

All three modes work against the same API surface. The identity provider is recorded in the audit trail so you can always trace who authorized a request.



Clerk SSO (production)

Clerk handles authentication for workspace users. Supported providers: Google, GitHub, Microsoft, and email/password.

Setup

Set three environment variables:

CLERK_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...
CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_live_...
CLERK_DOMAIN=your-app.clerk.accounts.dev

Users sign in through the workspace UI at http://localhost:4000 (self-hosted) or https://raptor.dev (cloud). Clerk issues a __session JWT cookie that Raptor validates on every request.

How it works


User signs in via Clerk's hosted UI (OAuth or email).
Clerk sets a __session cookie containing a signed JWT.
Raptor validates the JWT against your Clerk domain on every API call.
The user's Clerk ID, tenant, and role are extracted and recorded in governance events.


No application code is needed -- the browser handles the cookie automatically.

Without Clerk

If you omit all CLERK_* variables, Raptor runs in token-only mode. All API access uses API keys or the Founder Key. This is valid for self-hosted deployments that do not need SSO.



API keys

API keys are the primary method for programmatic access. Keys use the rpt_ prefix and are stored as SHA-256 hashes -- the plaintext key is shown exactly once at creation time.

title: Governance Model
description: How Raptor governs AI — from user input through classification, policy enforcement, proposal, and commit.
content:
Governance Model

Raptor interposes a deterministic governance layer between the user and AI execution. AI proposes. The governance core disposes. Nothing reaches the user or an external system without passing through deterministic checks.

Request lifecycle

Every user message follows the same path:


Classify — the classifier receives user input and categorizes intent into one of four types:

   - respond — conversational reply, no side effects
   - ask — clarification needed before proceeding
   - propose_action — AI recommends an action that requires human confirmation
   - execute_confirmed_action — human has confirmed, execute the action


Enforce — governance middleware evaluates the classified request against:

   - Capabilities — does the tenant's active policy grant this operation?
   - Policies — do the rules allow this specific action?
   - Budgets — has the tenant exceeded step, provider call, or artifact limits?
   - Rate limits — is the request within per-tenant API thresholds?
   - Suspension — is the tenant currently suspended?

If any check fails, the request is blocked and an authorization_event is recorded to the hash chain.


Propose — the AI generates a response in the proposal layer. At this stage, the output is structured but uncommitted. The AI handles language, reasoning, and recommendation — it does not handle authorization or execution.



Commit — the deterministic commit layer takes the proposal and:

   - Assigns trust boundaries to every segment (Confirmed, Executed, Retrieved, Likely, Uncertain)
   - Applies the weakest-link rule for the response-level boundary
   - Generates decision support metadata (confidence, recommendation, basis, risk)
   - Hashes the payload and chains it to the previous event
   - Records the execution event to the immutable audit log


Deliver — the committed, classified, hash-chained response reaches the user.


What makes this deterministic

The governance layer does not use AI to make governance decision

title: Trust Boundaries
description: The five trust levels that classify every segment of every Raptor response.
content:
Trust Boundaries

Every segment of every Raptor response carries a trust boundary — a classification that tells you how much you can rely on that specific claim.

The five boundaries

Confirmed (C)

Color: Gold | Meaning: Verified against an authoritative source.

The claim was checked against a database query, signed attestation, verified document, or audited record. The verification is recorded in the event log with source, query, and timestamp. Safe for operational decisions.

Example: "Q2 revenue was $4.2M" — verified via database query.

Executed (X)

Color: Teal | Meaning: Action ran with recorded result.

An action was actually performed — an API call made, a state transition recorded, a workflow completed. The execution is in the hash-chained event log with input, output, and timestamps.

Example: "Alert #7 acknowledged" — PBC action executed via API.

Retrieved (R)

Color: Purple | Meaning: Fetched from a system of record.

Data was pulled from a known source and presented as-is. The retrieval is recorded, but the content was not independently verified. Trustworthy to the degree the source is trustworthy.

Example: "Current alerts: 3 open" — retrieved from the alert system.

Likely (L)

Color: Slate blue | Meaning: High-confidence inference, not directly verified.

The AI's assessment based on context and reasoning. Not verified against an authoritative source. Confidence is high but the claim could be wrong. Independent verification recommended.

Example: "Renewal probability is 85-90%" — inferred from usage patterns.

Uncertain (U)

Color: Warm gray | Meaning: Limited evidence, treat with caution.

The AI is extrapolating beyond its context. Do not act without independent verification. The uncertainty is an honest signal, not a failure.

Example: "Market conditions may shift in Q4" — speculative.

title: Hash Chain
description: How Raptor's immutable audit chain ensures every output is traceable and tamper-evident.
content:
Hash Chain

Every governed operation in Raptor produces an execution event that is linked to the previous event via cryptographic hashing. This creates a tamper-evident chain — if any event is modified after the fact, the chain breaks.

How it works


Every chat turn, action execution, and governance decision creates an execution_event
Each event contains a payload (the full structured output) that is canonically hashed (SHA-256, deterministic JSON serialization, sorted keys)
Each event's event_hash includes the previous_event_hash, creating a linked chain
Database triggers prevent UPDATE and DELETE on the execution_events table


What's in an event

{
  "id": "uuid",
  "tenant_id": "uuid",
  "nest_id": "uuid",
  "event_type": "output_committed",
  "event_hash": "sha256:abc123...",
  "previous_event_hash": "sha256:def456...",
  "payload": {
    "trust_boundary": { "primary": "inferred", "route_type": "chat" },
    "segments": [...],
    "evidence_refs": [...]
  },
  "created_at": "2026-05-20T17:44:24Z"
}

Verification


Per-nest: GET /api/nests/{id}/verification checks chain integrity and returns claim-level freshness
Per-execution: GET /api/executions/{id}/trace returns the full event chain with hash verification
Tenant-wide: GET /api/tenant/audit/export exports the complete audit trail


Immutability guarantees

11 tables in Raptor are protected by database-level triggers that prevent modification:


execution_events — the primary hash chain
build_attestations — Ed25519 signed build proofs
transparency_log — public transparency records
authorization_events — governance decision audit trail
governance_policies — append-only policy lifecycle


This is not application-level protection — it's database-level enforcement that cannot be bypassed by application code.

Canonical hashing

Raptor uses canonical hashing to ensure identical inputs always produce identical hashes:


JSON keys are sorted alphabetically
No whitespace in serialized form
Numbers use their canonical

title: Decision Support
description: How Raptor provides structured guidance — confidence levels, recommendations, risk assessment.
content:
Decision Support

Every governed response includes a decision_support object that provides structured guidance for the operator.

Confidence levels

The classifier assigns a numeric confidence (0.0-1.0) which maps to a categorical level:

| Level | Threshold | Meaning | Recommendation behavior ||-------|-----------|---------|------------------------|| CLEAR | >= 95% | Evidence overwhelmingly supports one path | Direct recommendation provided || RECOMMENDED | >= 80% | Strong evidence, minor uncertainty | Recommendation with basis || ADVISORY | >= 50% | Evidence supports direction but alternatives exist | Options presented with tradeoffs || INSUFFICIENT | 

Response structure

{
  "decision_support": {
    "confidence": "RECOMMENDED",
    "recommendation": "Proceed with canary deployment.",
    "basis": "All preconditions verified, artifact integrity confirmed.",
    "risk_if_wrong": "Rollback requires manual intervention (~15m).",
    "alternatives": ["Run rollback rehearsal first (adds ~5m)"]
  }
}

Fields


confidence — categorical level (not the raw number)
recommendation — single-sentence directive. Empty when confidence is INSUFFICIENT.
basis — why you should trust this recommendation. Evidence-grounded, not conversational.
risk_if_wrong — what breaks if the recommendation is incorrect. Empty when risk is negligible.
alternatives — 0-3 alternative approaches. Empty when there's one clear path.


Confidence rules

The decision engine applies automatic confidence rules:


Below 0.5: Proposed actions are downgraded to conversational responses
0.5 to 0.79: Proposed actions are downgraded to clarification requests
0.8 and above: Actions proceed normally through the confirmation gate


These rules prevent the system from proposing actions it isn't confident about.

Actionability

The trust_boundary.actionability field summarizes whether to act:


safe — verified claims + CLEAR confidence: act with confidence
review — mixed boundaries: review before acting
blocked — in

title: Governance Policies
description: How Raptor policies control what AI can do — signed, versioned, deterministic enforcement.
content:
Governance Policies

Policies are the rules that govern what Raptor's AI is permitted to do. They are signed with Ed25519, versioned, and applied deterministically to every governed operation.

Policy lifecycle


Author — define rules (operations, actions, capabilities, budgets)
Sign — cryptographically sign the policy JSON
Activate — make it the active policy (previous version superseded)
Evaluate — every governed request checks the active policy
Supersede — when a new version activates, old versions are preserved in history


Policies are append-only. Old versions are never deleted — they're marked superseded and remain in the audit trail.

Policy structure

{
  "name": "deployment_governance",
  "version": 3,
  "mode": "enforced",
  "rules": [
    {
      "operation": "*",
      "action": "allow",
      "capabilities": ["chat:execute"],
      "max_steps": 1000,
      "max_provider_calls": 100
    },
    {
      "operation": "artifact_export",
      "action": "deny",
      "capabilities": []
    }
  ]
}

Modes


Enforced — policy violations block the operation (403 with reason)
Permissive — violations are logged but not blocked (monitoring mode)


Start with permissive to understand what your AI is doing, then switch to enforced when ready.

Built-in enforcement

Every governed request passes through:


Rate limit — per-tenant API/provider limits
Tenant suspension check — suspended tenants cannot execute
Capability check — does the operation require a capability the policy grants?
Budget check — max steps, provider calls, artifacts per operation
Policy evaluation — does the active policy allow this operation?


If any check fails, the request is blocked and an authorization_event is recorded.

API endpoints

POST /api/admin/policies/validate    — validate policy JSON
POST /api/admin/policies/sign        — sign and store a policy
POST /api/admin/policies/{id}/activate — activate a signed policy
POST /api/admin/policies/rollback    — rollback to previous version

title: Proposal/Commit Architecture
description: Why Raptor separates AI proposals from deterministic commits — and why that separation is the safety model.
content:
Proposal/Commit Architecture

Raptor enforces a hard separation between what AI proposes and what the system commits. AI is never directly connected to execution. This is not a design preference — it is the safety architecture.

The separation

Three layers handle three concerns:

| Layer | Responsibility | Deterministic? ||-------|---------------|----------------|| Proposal | AI generates language, recommendations, action suggestions | No — AI is probabilistic || Governance | Classify intent, enforce policies, check authorization | Yes — rule evaluation || Commit | Structure output, assign trust boundaries, hash-chain, execute | Yes — deterministic core |

The AI layer never touches execution directly. A proposed action passes through governance evaluation and human confirmation before the commit layer executes it.

How a proposed action flows


User says: "Deploy the canary build"
Classifier categorizes intent as propose_action
AI generates a structured proposal:

      {
     "action": "deploy_canary",
     "parameters": { "build_id": "b-4a91", "target": "staging" },
     "reasoning": "Build passed all gates. Canary deploy is next step."
   }

Governance checks: does the policy allow deploy_canary? Is the user authorized? Is the budget within limits?
Proposal is presented to the user with decision support metadata
User confirms
Classifier re-categorizes as execute_confirmed_action
Commit layer executes the action and records the result to the hash chain


If the user does not confirm, the action is never executed. The proposal remains in the audit trail as a proposed-but-not-confirmed event.

What this prevents

Prompt injection leading to execution. Even if an attacker manipulates the AI into proposing a harmful action, the governance layer evaluates the proposal against policies, and the human confirmation gate blocks unauthorized execution.

title: Nests
description: The primary object in Raptor — a governed conversation session holding memory, governance, provenance, and execution state.
content:
Nests

A nest is a governed conversation session. It is the primary object in Raptor — not a feature inside a larger container, but the unit around which everything else is organized.

Every nest holds:


Chat history — the full conversation between user and AI
Actions and proposals — proposed actions, confirmation state, execution results
Execution events — the hash-chained audit trail for this session
Artifacts — files, documents, and generated outputs
Governance events — policy evaluations, authorization decisions, trust assignments
Memory — context that persists across turns within the session


Creating a nest

A new nest starts with a clean governance state: no prior context, no inherited trust claims, fresh policy evaluation. The tenant's active governance policy applies from the first turn.

POST /api/nests
{
  "title": "Q2 deployment review",
  "metadata": { "team": "platform", "priority": "high" }
}

Nests can be created through the API or through the Control Panel interface. Every nest is tenant-scoped — it belongs to exactly one organization and is subject to that organization's RLS policies.

Nest lifecycle

Nests move through three states:

| State | Meaning ||-------|---------|| Active | Open for conversation, actions, and governance operations || Archived | Read-only. Full audit trail preserved. No new operations. || Forked | A new nest created from an existing one, continuing from a specific intent |

Archiving

Archived nests retain their complete hash chain, governance history, and artifacts. Archiving is a governance event recorded in the audit trail. Archived nests can be read and exported but not modified.

Forking

Forking creates a new nest that inherits context from the source nest. The fork point is recorded as a governance event in both the source and the new nest. The new nest starts its own hash chain — it references the source but does not extend it.

title: Temporal Trust
description: How Raptor tracks claim freshness — because a verified fact from last week is not the same as a verified fact from five minutes ago.
content:
Temporal Trust

A trust boundary tells you how a claim was established. Temporal trust tells you whether that claim is still current. Both matter for operational decisions.

Freshness states

Every claim in Raptor carries a freshness state that updates automatically based on the time elapsed since verification:

| State | Meaning | Operator guidance ||-------|---------|-------------------|| FRESH | Within the source-specific freshness window | Act with confidence || AGING | Past 50% of the freshness window | Still valid, re-verification approaching || STALE | Exceeded the freshness window | Do not act without re-verification || INVALIDATED | Contradicted by newer evidence | Discard — newer evidence supersedes |

Freshness transitions are automatic. When a FRESH claim crosses the 50% threshold of its window, it becomes AGING. When it exceeds the window, it becomes STALE. No manual intervention required.

Source-specific windows

Different types of evidence go stale at different rates. Raptor defines freshness windows per source type:

| Source type | Freshness window | Rationale ||-------------|-----------------|-----------|| Execution events | 1 hour | System state changes rapidly after actions || Database queries | 4 hours | Operational data shifts through the day || Policy evaluations | 24 hours | Policies change infrequently || Attestations | 7 days | Signed attestations are durable evidence || External API responses | 1 hour | Third-party data has unknown update frequency |

These windows are defaults. Organizations can configure custom windows per source type through governance policies.

How freshness affects decisions

Temporal trust integrates with decision support. When stale claims are present in a response:


Decision confidence is reduced. A response grounded in stale evidence cannot produce a CLEAR confidence level regardless of other factors.
Actionability is downgraded. Stale claims shift the actionability from safe to review, signaling the operator t

title: Multi-Provider Architecture
description: How Raptor abstracts AI providers behind a unified interface — provider-agnostic governance with built-in failover.
content:
Multi-Provider Architecture

Raptor is not tied to a single AI provider. A unified Provider interface abstracts Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, and Together AI behind a common contract. The governance layer does not care which model produced the response — the same trust boundaries, policies, and audit chain apply regardless.

Supported providers

| Provider | Models | Use case ||----------|--------|----------|| Anthropic | Claude family | Primary reasoning and governance || OpenAI | GPT family | Alternative reasoning, specialized tasks || Gemini | Gemini family | Multi-modal, alternative reasoning || Together AI | Open-source models | Cost optimization, specialized inference |

The Provider interface

Every provider implements the same interface:

interface Provider {
  chat(messages: Message[], options: ProviderOptions): Promise<ProviderResponse>
  healthCheck(): Promise<HealthStatus>
  estimateCost(messages: Message[]): CostEstimate
}

This means the governance middleware, commit layer, and trust boundary classifier interact with a single abstraction. Adding a new provider means implementing this interface — no changes to governance logic.

Provider selection

Provider selection is configured at the tenant level:


Primary provider — handles all requests by default
Fallback provider — activated when the primary is unhealthy or rate-limited
Per-operation override — specific operations can target specific providers


The selection is deterministic. There is no AI-driven routing — the tenant configuration specifies which provider handles which operations.

Health monitoring

Each provider connection is monitored:


Latency tracking — rolling average response time
Error rate — percentage of failed requests over a sliding window
Rate limit state — remaining capacity within the provider's rate limits
Circuit breaker — provider is marked unhealthy after consecutive failures, with automatic recovery checks

title: Multi-Tenant Isolation
description: How Raptor enforces tenant boundaries — row-level security, scoped resources, and the guarantee that data never crosses organizations.
content:
Multi-Tenant Isolation

Every Raptor account maps to one organization. Tenant isolation is enforced at the database level, not the application level. Data never crosses tenant boundaries.

Row-level security

Every table that holds tenant data includes a tenant_id column. PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) policies ensure that queries can only access rows belonging to the authenticated tenant.

This is not application-level filtering (a WHERE clause that could be forgotten). RLS is enforced by the database engine itself. Even if application code contains a bug that omits the tenant filter, the database rejects the query.

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON execution_events
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant_id')::uuid);

Every API request sets the tenant context before executing any query. The database enforces the boundary from that point forward.

Tenant-scoped resources

The following resources are scoped to a single tenant and cannot be accessed across boundaries:

| Resource | Scope ||----------|-------|| Nests | Conversations, memory, governance state || Execution events | The complete hash-chained audit trail || Governance policies | Active and historical policy versions || API keys | Authentication credentials || Webhooks | Event notification endpoints || Artifacts | Files, documents, generated outputs || Billing | Usage tracking, provider costs, invoices || RBAC assignments | Role and permission grants |

Identity mapping

Raptor uses Clerk for authentication and organization management. Each Clerk organization maps to exactly one Raptor tenant:


Clerk handles user authentication, SSO, and session management
Raptor maps the Clerk organization ID to a tenant_id
Users belong to a Clerk organization and inherit the corresponding tenant context
A user in multiple Clerk organizations accesses each as a separate Raptor tenant


Identity is externalized. Governance is internal. Raptor never stores passwords or manages authentication flows di

REST API Integration

Connect any backend or frontend to Raptor's governance substrate over HTTP. This guide walks through authentication, your first governed message, interpreting trust boundaries, and querying the audit trail.

Prerequisites


A running Raptor instance (cloud at https://raptor.harpyits.com or self-hosted at http://localhost:4000)
An API key (created via Settings UI or the /api/keys endpoint)


1. Authenticate

Raptor API keys use the rpt_ prefix. Pass them in the Authorization header or the X-Raptor-Key header:

# Option A: Bearer token
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer rpt_a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6" \
  https://raptor.harpyits.com/api/nests

Option B: X-Raptor-Key header

  https://raptor.harpyits.com/api/nests

Include the API version header on every request:

-H "X-Raptor-API-Version: 2026-05-09"

title: Pattern 1: Governance Wrapper
description: Add Raptor governance around your existing AI application with minimal code changes.
content:
Pattern 1: Governance Wrapper

The simplest integration — wrap your existing AI calls with Raptor's governance layer.

When to use


You have an existing AI application that works
You need governance, audit trails, and trust boundaries
You don't want to change your AI orchestration logic


Architecture

Your App → Raptor API → Your AI Provider
                ↓
         Governance check
         Trust boundary assignment
         Hash-chained audit event
                ↓
         Structured response back to your app

Integration

1. Route your AI calls through Raptor

Instead of calling your provider directly:

// Before: direct to provider
const response = await anthropic.messages.create({ ... });

// After: through Raptorconst response = await fetch('https://your-raptor.com/api/chat', {  method: 'POST',  headers: {    'Authorization': 'Bearer rpt_your_api_key',    'Content-Type': 'application/json'  },  body: JSON.stringify({ message: userInput })});

2. Read the trust boundary

const data = await response.json();

// Every response tells you how much to trust itif (data.trust_boundary.actionability.level === 'safe') {  // Safe to act on  showToUser(data.reply);} else if (data.trust_boundary.actionability.level === 'blocked') {  // Needs review  escalateToHuman(data.reply, data.trust_boundary);}

3. Use the audit trail

Every response is automatically logged in the hash-chained event store. Query it:

GET /api/nests/{nestId}/governance    # Governance decisions
GET /api/executions/{id}/trace        # Full execution chain
GET /api/tenant/audit/export          # Complete audit export

What you get


Trust boundaries on every response (no code changes to your AI logic)
Hash-chained audit trail (every response traceable)
Governance enforcement (policies control what AI can do)
Decision support (confidence levels, recommendations)
Billing metering (per governed response)

title: Pattern 2: Orchestration
description: Use Raptor as the decision layer in a multi-agent AI system.
content:
Pattern 2: Orchestration

title: Webhook Integration
description: Receive real-time governance events from Raptor via HMAC-signed webhook deliveries.
content:
Webhook Integration

Raptor dispatches webhook events when governance decisions, responses, and policy changes occur. Each delivery is signed with HMAC-SHA256 so your endpoint can verify authenticity.

1. Create a webhook endpoint

Register a URL and subscribe to the events you care about:

curl -X POST https://raptor.harpyits.com/api/webhooks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer rpt_your_key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "url": "https://your-app.com/webhooks/raptor",
    "events": ["governance.allowed", "governance.denied", "response.created"]
  }'

The response includes a whsec_ prefixed signing secret. Store it securely — it is shown only at creation:

{
  "ok": true,
  "endpoint": {
    "id": "uuid",
    "url": "https://your-app.com/webhooks/raptor",
    "events": ["governance.allowed", "governance.denied", "response.created"],
    "secret": "whsec_a1b2c3d4e5f6...",
    "active": true
  }
}

Pass an empty events array to subscribe to all event types.

2. Verify HMAC-SHA256 signatures

Every webhook delivery includes two headers:

| Header | Contents ||---|---|| X-Raptor-Event | Event type (e.g. governance.allowed) || X-Raptor-Signature | HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of the request body, keyed with your endpoint secret |

Verify the signature before processing:

import crypto from "node:crypto";

function verifySignature(body, secret, receivedSignature) {  const expected = crypto    .createHmac("sha256", secret)    .update(body)    .digest("hex");  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(    Buffer.from(expected, "hex"),    Buffer.from(receivedSignature, "hex")  );}

Always use a constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks.

3. Event types

| Event | Fired when ||---|---|| governance.allowed | A governance decision permits an operation || governance.denied | A governance decision blocks an operation || response.created | A governed response is committed to the audit chain || execution.completed | A confirmed action finishes executing || policy.activated

description: Create, scope, rotate, and revoke Raptor API keys for backend and CI integrations.
content:
API Key Management

Raptor API keys authenticate backend services, CI pipelines, and SDK integrations. Keys use the rpt_ prefix and are stored as SHA-256 hashes — the plaintext key is shown exactly once at creation.

1. Create a key

Via API

curl -X POST https://raptor.harpyits.com/api/keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer your_clerk_jwt" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "production-backend",
    "scopes": ["all"],
    "expires_at": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z"
  }'

Response:

{
  "ok": true,
  "key": "rpt_a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6",
  "key_id": "uuid",
  "name": "production-backend",
  "prefix": "rpt_a1b2",
  "warning": "Store this key securely. It will not be shown again."
}

Copy the key value immediately. After this response, Raptor only stores the hash — there is no way to retrieve the full key.

Via Settings UI


Open the Control Panel
Navigate to Settings
Click "Create API Key"
Name the key and set optional expiration
Copy the displayed key before closing the dialog


2. Key format

Keys follow the format rpt_ + 32 hex characters:

rpt_a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6

The first 8 characters (rpt_a1b2) are stored as a prefix for identification in the key list. The full key is never stored — only its SHA-256 hash.

3. Authentication

Use the key in either header:

# Authorization header
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer rpt_a1b2c3d4..." \
  https://raptor.harpyits.com/api/chat

X-Raptor-Key header
curl -H "X-Raptor-Key: rpt_a1b2c3d4..." \
  https://raptor.harpyits.com/api/chat

Keys inherit the permissions of the tenant that created them. Every request made with a key is attributed to the creating actor and tenant.

4. Scoping

Keys accept a scopes array at creation. If omitted, the default scope is ["all"].

{
  "name": "read-only-dashboard",
  "scopes": ["read"]
}

Scoped keys can only perform operations matching their granted scopes. Use narrow scopes for integrations that only need read access.

Each authorization event records a governance decision:

{

  "operation": "chat_execution",
  "decision": "allowed",
  "reason": "policy_rule_matched",
  "policy_mode": "enforced",
  "correlation_id": "uuid",

title: Database
description: PostgreSQL setup, schema migrations, backup/restore, and data retention for self-hosted Raptor.
content:
Database

Raptor uses PostgreSQL 16+ as its sole data store. In a containerized closed environment, any PostgreSQL 16+ database can be designated via the DATABASE_URL environment variable. The Docker Compose bundle includes a PostgreSQL 16 Alpine container, but you can point Raptor at any compatible instance: managed (Neon, RDS, Cloud SQL, Supabase), self-hosted, or local.

Connection

Set the DATABASE_URL environment variable to a standard PostgreSQL connection string:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@host:5432/raptor?sslmode=require

For the bundled Docker Compose setup, this is configured automatically using the POSTGRES_PASSWORD variable.

Connection Pooling

For production deployments with multiple control-panel instances or high concurrency, place a connection pooler (PgBouncer, Supavisor, or your managed provider's built-in pooler) between Raptor and PostgreSQL. Raptor uses standard database/sql connection pooling internally, but an external pooler helps when:


Running multiple control-panel replicas
Database connections are limited (managed tiers)
You need connection-level observability


When using an external pooler, ensure it operates in transaction mode (not session mode) for compatibility with Raptor's query patterns.

Schema Migrations

Migrations run automatically on startup. The Docker Compose bundle includes a dedicated migrate container (using golang-migrate) that:


Waits for PostgreSQL to pass its health check
Applies all pending migrations from the /migrations directory
Exits successfully
Only then does the control-panel container start


Migration files are numbered sequentially (001_enums.up.sql, 002_tables.up.sql, etc.) and are idempotent. The migration tool tracks applied versions in a schema_migrations table.

Running Migrations Manually

If you run Raptor outside Docker Compose, apply migrations before starting the binary:

# Using golang-migrate CLI
migrate -path ./migrations \
  -database "postgresql://raptor:password@localhost:

content:
AI Providers

Raptor acts as a governance layer between your application and AI providers. It does not host models. You supply provider API keys, and Raptor routes inference requests through its governance engine before forwarding them to the provider.

Supported Providers

| Provider | Environment Variable | Models ||---|---|---|| Anthropic | ANTHROPIC_API_KEY | Claude 4 Opus, Claude 4 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 family || OpenAI | OPENAI_API_KEY | GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o1, o3 family || Google | GEMINI_API_KEY | Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash family || Together AI | TOGETHER_API_KEY | Llama, Mixtral, open-weight models |

At least one provider key is required. Set the corresponding environment variable and Raptor detects the provider at startup.

Configuration

Add provider keys to your .env file:

# Set one or more
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
GEMINI_API_KEY=AIza...
TOGETHER_API_KEY=...

Restart the control-panel after changing provider keys:

docker compose restart control-panel

Verifying Provider Status

Check which providers are active and healthy:

curl http://localhost:4000/api/runtime/config

The response includes the list of configured providers and their status. Use this endpoint for monitoring dashboards and alerting.

Multi-Provider Failover

Primary routing: Requests specify a model (e.g., claude-sonnet-4-20250514). Raptor routes to the corresponding provider.

This guide covers everything required to run Raptor in production. Work through each section before exposing the deployment to real traffic.

Environment

Set RAPTOR_ENV=production. This enables:


Strict authentication enforcement

content:
Operations

This section covers everything you need to keep a Raptor instance healthy in production. The core operational loop is: monitor health, deploy via git push, back up the database, and verify integrity.

Health Monitoring

Raptor exposes three health endpoints out of the box:

| Endpoint | Purpose ||---|---|| /api/health | Liveness -- is the process running? || /api/ready | Readiness -- is the database connected and are migrations applied? || /api/health/dependencies | Per-dependency health breakdown |

Point your uptime monitor at /api/ready. If it returns anything other than {"status": "ready"}, the instance should not receive traffic.

For deeper operational metrics -- connection pool utilization, request rates, error rates, and provider health -- see the Monitoring guide.

Deployment

Raptor deploys via git push only. Direct deploy commands (such as railway up) bypass the build attestation pipeline and break provenance. The correct workflow:

git push origin main

The CI pipeline builds the image, signs it with Ed25519 attestation, and deploys. Migrations run automatically on startup via the migrate container.

For Docker Compose environments:

git pull
docker compose build
docker compose up -d

See the Upgrade guide for versioning, rollback, and breaking-change policy.

After any restore, verify hash chain integrity and governance table counts before accepting traffic. Immutable governance tables must never be modified in place -- restore from backup only.

Full procedures are in the Backup and Restore guide.

Integrity Verification

title: Backup and Restore
description: Database backup strategies, restore procedures, and post-restore verification for self-hosted and cloud Raptor deployments.
content:
Backup and Restore

Raptor's governance data lives in PostgreSQL. The backup strategy depends on your deployment model. Both paths converge on the same post-restore verification process.

Critical rule: Immutable governance tables (events, attestations, hash chain entries) must never be modified in place. If data is corrupted or missing, restore from backup. Manual edits to immutable tables break the hash chain and invalidate the governance audit trail.

Self-Hosted: pg_dump

Full Backup

pg_dump -h localhost -U raptor -d raptor_db \
  --format=custom \
  --file=raptor_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).dump

Use --format=custom for compressed, restorable output. Schedule this via cron to meet your RPO target (recommended: every hour or less).

Example cron entry for hourly backups with 7-day retention:

0     pg_dump -h localhost -U raptor -d raptor_db \
  --format=custom \
  --file=/backups/raptor_$(date +\%Y\%m\%d_\%H\%M\%S).dump \
  && find /backups -name "raptor_.dump" -mtime +7 -delete

Full Restore

# Stop the control-panel to prevent writes during restore
docker compose stop control-panel

Restore from backup

Upgrades

Raptor uses date-based versioning and automatic migrations. Upgrades are designed to be low-risk: pull the new image, restart, and verify health.

Versioning

Raptor versions follow a date-based scheme: YYYY-MM-DD (for example, 2026-05-09). Each version corresponds to a tagged release and a container image.


Patch releases (same date, incremented suffix like 2026-05-09.1) contain bug fixes only.
Minor releases (new date) may add features, endpoints, or configuration options. Existing behavior does not change.
Breaking releases are rare and announced in advance. See Breaking Changes Policy below.


Upgrade Procedure

Docker Compose

# Pull the latest code
git pull origin main

Rebuild images
docker compose build

Restart services (migrations run automatically)
docker compose up -d

Railway

Deploy via git push. Railway rebuilds the image and restarts the service automatically.

git push origin main

Do not use railway up or equivalent direct-deploy commands. They bypass build attestation and break provenance.

Verify After Upgrade

# Check readiness
curl http://localhost:4000/api/ready

Check integrity (build attestation matches new version)
curl http://localhost:4000/api/runtime/integrity \
  -H "X-Raptor-Token: your-access-token"

content:
Security Architecture

Raptor's security model is built into the substrate, not bolted on after the fact. Authentication, authorization, data isolation, cryptographic integrity, and privacy controls are structural — they operate at the database and middleware layers, not the application layer alone.

Authentication

Raptor supports three authentication modes. Each serves a different operational context.

Clerk SSO (Production)

For workspace users signing in through the Control Panel UI.


OAuth 2.0 via Clerk with Google, GitHub, and Microsoft identity providers
JWT verification on every request using Clerk's published JWKS
Session tokens include tenant binding — a user's Clerk organization maps to exactly one Raptor tenant
Token expiration and refresh handled by Clerk's session management


Required variables: CLERK_SECRET_KEY, CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY, CLERK_DOMAIN

API Keys (Infrastructure)

For programmatic access via the REST API.


Keys are prefixed with rpt_ for identification
Only the SHA-256 hash is stored in the database — the plaintext key is shown once at creation and never again
Each key is scoped to a single tenant and carries an explicit set of permissions
Keys can be configured with credit-exhaustion behavior: pause requests or continue with degraded service


Founder Key (Bootstrap)

For initial setup and emergency access before Clerk is configured.


Set via RAPTOR_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable
Authenticated using SHA-256 constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks
Grants full access to the tenant — intended for bootstrap, not production operation
Should be rotated or disabled once Clerk SSO is configured


Authorization

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

Every authenticated user or API key is assigned a role within their tenant. Three roles govern access:

Threat Model

This document describes the attack surfaces Raptor is designed to resist, the mitigations in place, and the trust assumptions the system makes.

Attack Surfaces

API Endpoint Abuse

Threat: An attacker sends malformed, high-volume, or crafted requests to public API endpoints to exhaust resources, extract data, or bypass governance.

Mitigations:


Per-tenant rate limiting enforced at the middleware layer
Input validation on all API endpoints before governance processing
Structured error responses that do not leak internal state
All requests require authentication — there are no anonymous API endpoints except health checks and .well-known public verification endpoints


Authentication Bypass

Threat: An attacker attempts to forge JWTs, steal API keys, or exploit the Founder Key to gain unauthorized access.

Mitigations:


JWT: Verified against Clerk's published JWKS on every request. Expired tokens are rejected. Token claims are validated against the tenant binding.
API keys: Only SHA-256 hashes are stored. A database breach does not expose usable credentials. Keys are prefixed (rpt_) for easy identification and rotation.
Founder Key: Compared using constant-time comparison (SHA-256) to prevent timing attacks. Intended for bootstrap only — should be rotated once Clerk is configured.
Grace period: Authentication transitions (e.g., Clerk configuration changes) include a grace period to prevent lockouts, with explicit logging of grace-period authentications.


Provider Compromise

Threat: A compromised or malicious AI provider returns manipulated responses designed to bypass governance, exfiltrate data, or inject harmful content.

Mitigations:


Trust boundaries reflect verification status, not provider claims. A provider's response is classified based on what Raptor can verify (Confirmed, Retrieved) versus what it cannot (Likely, Uncertain). Provider self-reported confidence is not trusted.

Webhooks API

The Webhooks API lets you subscribe to governance events in real time. Raptor delivers events to your HTTPS endpoint with HMAC-SHA256 signatures for verification.

Event Types

| Event | Fired when ||-------|-----------|| governance.allowed | A governance evaluation permitted an action || governance.denied | A governance evaluation denied an action || response.created | A governed response was delivered || execution.completed | A workflow execution finished || policy.activated | A new policy was activated |

Delivery

Each webhook delivery includes:


HMAC-SHA256 signature in the X-Raptor-Signature header, computed over the raw request body using your webhook secret.
Retry on failure: Raptor retries failed deliveries (non-2xx response or timeout) with exponential backoff up to 3 attempts over 1 hour.
Timeout: Your endpoint must respond within 10 seconds.


Signature Verification

import hmac
import hashlib

def verify_signature(payload_body: bytes, secret: str, signature: str) -> bool:    expected = hmac.new(        secret.encode("utf-8"),        payload_body,        hashlib.sha256    ).hexdigest()    return hmac.compare_digest(f"sha256={expected}", signature)

Troubleshooting

This guide covers the most common issues you will encounter when running Raptor, organized by category. Each issue includes the symptom, likely cause, and fix steps.

Authentication

401 Unauthorized — Expired JWT

Symptom: API requests return 401 with "error": "token_expired".

Cause: The Clerk session token has expired and the client has not refreshed it.

Fix:


If using the Control Panel UI, sign out and sign back in.
If using a custom client, ensure your Clerk SDK is configured to refresh tokens automatically.
Check that your server's clock is synchronized (NTP). JWT validation is time-sensitive.


401 Unauthorized — Missing API Key

Symptom: API requests return 401 with "error": "missing_credentials".

Cause: The request does not include an authentication header.

Fix:


For API key authentication, include the header: Authorization: Bearer rpt_your_key
For Founder Key authentication, include the header: X-Raptor-Token: your_access_token
Verify the key exists and has not been revoked in Settings > API Keys.


401 Unauthorized — Clerk Misconfiguration

Symptom: All Clerk-authenticated requests return 401. API key requests work fine.

Cause: Clerk environment variables are missing or incorrect.

Fix:


Verify these environment variables are set:

   - CLERK_SECRET_KEY — starts with sk_live_ or sk_test_
   - CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY — starts with pk_live_ or pk_test_
   - CLERK_DOMAIN — your Clerk domain (e.g., your-app.clerk.accounts.dev)

Ensure the Clerk application's JWT template matches Raptor's expected claims.
Restart the Raptor process after changing environment variables.


401 Unauthorized — Grace Period

Symptom: Requests return 401 intermittently during an authentication configuration change.

Cause: Raptor includes a grace period during authentication transitions. If you are seeing 401 errors during this window, the new configuration may be invalid.

How long can records be retained?

It depends on the table type.


Immutable tables (execution events, build attestations, transparency log, authorization events, governance policies): indefinitely. These tables form the cryptographic hash chain and cannot be deleted without breaking chain integrity. There is no retention limit.
Mutable tables (conversations, uploads, cache, artifacts): configurable per tenant. Retention periods range from 30 days to indefinite. Auto-delete can be enabled per resource type via retention policies.


You configure retention policies in Settings > Privacy > Retention Policies.

What database does Raptor need?

PostgreSQL 16 or later. Any PostgreSQL instance will work — self-managed, AWS RDS, Google Cloud SQL, Railway, Supabase, Neon, or a local Docker container.

Raptor connects via a standard DATABASE_URL connection string:

postgresql://user:password@host:port/database

The database user needs permission to create tables, triggers, and enable Row-Level Security. Raptor runs its own migrations on startup.

Can I use my own AI providers?

Yes. Raptor uses a Bring Your Own Provider (BYOP) model.

You supply your own API keys for any supported provider — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, or Together AI. Raptor routes requests to your chosen provider using your key. You pay the provider directly at their published rates.

Raptor charges a governance fee of $0.012 per governed response for the classification, policy enforcement, trust boundary assignment, and hash-chained audit trail. The governance fee is the same regardless of which provider you use or what the provider charges.
